subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Adjustment Failure
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Adjustment Failure.

hook.text: Guess the product of 8x7x6x5x4x3x2x1 in five seconds. Most guess 2,250. The answer is 40,320.

buildup.text: Starting from 8 and failing to adjust enough is a classic anchoring-and-adjustment failure.

discovery.text: We start from an anchor and adjust, but adjustments are consistently too small. We stop too early.

twist.text: Reverse it to 1x2x3 up to 8. People guess even lower: 512. The starting anchor changes everything.

climax.text: Adjustment requires effort. Our lazy System 1 anchors and barely moves. The result is chronic underestimation.

punchline.text: Your first guess is an anchor. Adjust further.

quiz.question: Why do people underestimate 8x7x6x5x4x3x2x1?
options: They anchor on early numbers and adjust too little
The number is too large to imagine

details.summary: The adjustment failure occurs when people start from an anchor and adjust insufficiently toward the correct answer. The initial anchor is given too much weight, and the adjustment process stops prematurely, leaving the final estimate biased toward the starting point.
details.whyItMatters: Insufficient adjustment explains why anchoring is so powerful. People know they should adjust away from the anchor but consistently stop short.
takeaways: People adjust away from anchors but consistently stop before reaching the correct answer
The adjustment process is effortful and terminates when a plausible answer is reached
Greater cognitive load makes adjustment even more insufficient

faq.question: Why do people stop adjusting before reaching the correct answer?
faq.answer: Adjustment is a serial, effortful process that proceeds away from the anchor until a plausible value is reached. People stop at the first plausible answer rather than continuing to the most accurate one. The anchor defines the range of plausibility.

faq.question: How can decision-makers counteract insufficient adjustment?
faq.answer: Consider the opposite direction: if the anchor is high, ask what would make the answer low. Use multiple independent anchors and average them. Generate your own estimate before encountering any anchor. Allow more time for the adjustment process.
